rv.q: Yet you just cannot help but see "The Anarchist" as a cautionary tale for the writer who gains so much clout that he can now get anything up in the great American marketplace without any of the usual formative niceties, without any of the usual checks and balances.
David Mamet's new play 'The Anarchist' is a talky two-hander that pits a convicted terrorist against her parole officer in a battle of wits that generates more heat than light.
The two actresses, seated across from each other at a plain table, engage in a battle of wills that feels more like a philosophical exercise than a fully realized drama.
More needlessly opaque debate than drama
LuPone and Winger are both spectacular actresses, but they can't make David Mamet's sterile two-hander come alive.
For all the skill with which Ms. Peet has constructed her play, it remains stubbornly static.
No one talks like this and the two actresses struggle to make something unnatural seem natural.
Certainly, The Anarchist leaves no shortage of material for after-theater debate.
LuPone and Winger might just as well stand at lecterns, two deeply interesting, star-quality actors subsuming all that's interesting about them in service to brusque badinage between opaque symbols.
If you ask me, I'm still glad to have been part of the mob who demanded an original drama, but The Anarchist could have used a lot more blood and tears.
If only the same could be said of Mamet's play.

This simple setup surely could have made for a volatile, confrontational drama. But the 70-minute play is little more than a meandering and academic debate that’s hard to follow. While I won’t spoil the ending, let’s just say that it’s quick, random and heavy-handed, much like the rest of the play.
'The Anarchist' only runs 65 minutes, but I doubt there'll be any complaints that it's too short.
Even at just 70 intermissionless minutes, "The Anarchist" is a challenge to sentience.
Mamet certainly believes in punishing his audience.
